title: When 100 psychology studies were repeated, most failed to replicate
body: In 2015, a large collaboration led by Brian Nosek redid 100 studies from three leading psychology journals. Of 97 originals that had reported significant results, only about 36% gave significant results again, and effects were on average about half as large. Small samples, flexible analyses and a preference for striking results had let false or inflated findings through. The shock helped launch reforms such as pre-registration and large multi-lab studies.

slides.question: Of the 97 studies with significant results, what percentage gave significant results again?
slides.explanation: Only about 36%, and the effects were on average about half as large as first reported.

slides.heading: Of 97 significant findings, only about 36% were significant again
slides.note: Reproducibility Project: Psychology, 2015; effect sizes averaged half the original magnitude.

slides.heading: Famous casualties
slides.text: Ego depletion, the idea that willpower runs out like fuel, and the claim that power poses change your hormones have both struggled in careful replications.

slides.heading: How flukes get published
slides.text: Testing many measures and reporting only the ones that ‘worked’, or stopping data collection once results look good, can make chance noise look real.

slides.heading: The fix: pre-registration
slides.text: Researchers publish their hypothesis and analysis plan before collecting data, so results can’t be quietly reshaped afterwards.

slides.heading: Plenty survived
slides.text: Many findings hold up well, from anchoring to the spacing effect. The crisis is about separating solid results from shaky ones, not dismissing the field.

slides.heading: Which finding has held up well?
slides.explanation: Anchoring has replicated well in large projects. Ego depletion and the hormonal effects of power poses have struggled in careful replications.
